text.p: Sweden's former Ryder Cup player Joakim Haeggmann made the most of perfect early morning conditions to fire a course-record eight-under-par 63 as the Loch Lomond World Invitational began on Wednesday.

Haeggman birdied the last three holes to give him nine for the day along with an eagle against three dropped shots as he posted a target that was unlikely to be bettered on the 7,050-yard gem of a course beside the famous Scottish lake.

On a course his rivals Tom Lehman and Colin Montgomerie called "defenceless" in the calm conditions, Haeggman birdied five holes on the front nine without a blemish but dropped shots at three of the first six holes on the back nine after missing the greens with his approaches.
But his three closing birdies repaired the damage and he required only 27 putts in his round.

"That was the first time I've gone round in less that 33 putts in several weeks," he said. "There was no breeze, completely still and if a 63 was going to happen it was going to be early in the morning."
American Lehman, who will defend his British Open title at Royal Troon next week, compiled an excellent 65 that matched the old course record set last year by Frenchman Jean Van de Velde.
Lehman had only one practice round, finishing at 2200 local (2100 GMT) on Tuesday night because the plane bringing him to Scotland was delayed.
But he felt his lack of familiarity with the course cost him only one shot and he managed to go round without a bogey despite missing several makeable putts.
But Montgomerie, who won the Irish Open with a spectacular closing 62 on Sunday, could manage only a 69, two under par.
His putting let him down. "I created so many chances but I misread the putts and I didn't hole out well enough," he said.
Montgomerie, who played in the seventh three-man group, was upset by the slow pace of play among the earlier groups.
"We were given four hours 20 minutes to play. The first group took 4:16, fine but the second (Haeggman's group) took 4:36.
"So that set the pace and as a result of that we took 4:40. That's too slow on a lovely summer day. Slow play penalties are not being imposed."
Tournament director Mike Stewart was not immediately available for comment.
U.S. Open champion Ernie Els carded a one-under-par 70 composed of pars on the first 17 holes and a birdie three at the last.
Jose Maria Olazabal of Spain matched his score but looked to be headed for something better until he dropped three shots on the 15th and 16th holes.
Haeggman, who in 1993 became the first Swede to make the Ryder Cup team, had another 63 earlier in the year -- at the Cannes Open when he needed it to make the cut after an opening 83.
"I've played well this year but my putting had been poor and I've been getting a little fed up," he said.
"I was a little angry today after six holes because I was two under and I felt I could be four or five under. But I turned it around."
His eagle came at the long 13th where he hit a brilliant three-wood second shot to five feet and holed the putt.
Among the later starters in the impressive field were world number two Greg Norman, Nick Faldo of Britain, German Bernhard Langer and Ryder Cup captain Seve Ballesteros.
